data.text: Navigating Fremont's Roadways

Fremont’s roadway infrastructure continues to evolve to enhance safety and accessibility for all residents.  The City’s General Plan and Mobility Action Plan aims to increase walking and biking while reducing crashes involving vulnerable roadway users.  The City is committed to educating all roadway users on safely navigating these new infrastructure treatments, ensuring they can remain confident and secure while driving, biking, or walking.

The recent changes in Fremont’s roadways include the addition of roundabouts, protected intersections, protected bike lanes, street markings, and updated traffic signal systems.  These improvements are designed to reduce severe injury/fatal crashes and reduce vehicle speeds while optimizing vehicle traffic flow.  Learn more about the various roadway improvements and transportation projects below.
Pedestrian Crossings and Sidewalk Improvement Projects
Decoto Road Complete Streets﻿

This project will improve Decoto Road from just east of I-880 to Paseo Padre Parkway. It will implement transit-priority treatments to provide travel alternatives, ease congestion in the Dumbarton Corridor, and provide complete street upgrades to improve safety and access for bicyclists and pedestrians. (shown in light green)
Peralta Boulevard Complete Streets

The Peralta Boulevard project will improve segments of former State Route (SR) 84 relinquished from the State Department of Transportation (Caltrans) to the City of Fremont allowing for the repaving and implementation of "complete streets" improvements to enhance safety and mobility for all users, including drivers, pedestrians, bicyclists, schoolchildren, and businesses.
Mowry Avenue Complete Streets

The Mowry Avenue project will improve segments of former State Route (SR) 84 relinquished from the State Department of Transportation (Caltrans) to the City of Fremont allowing for the repaving and implementation of "complete streets" improvements to enhance safety and mobility for all users, including drivers, pedestrians, bicyclists, schoolchildren, and businesses.
Paseo Padre Parkway Complete Streets

Elements of the approved project scope will be implemented separately and in conjunction with similar citywide projects that address paving/striping, pedestrian crossing safety improvements, and new traffic signals.
Centerville Complete Streets Project
The project will feature significant roadway improvements, including:

• Sidewalk widening improvements and replacement
  • Raised and separated bikeway along Fremont Blvd between Thornton Ave. and Bonde Ave. 
  • Pavement rehabilitation
  • Upgraded traffic signal and protected intersection at Fremont Blvd./Thornton Ave.
  • Upgraded traffic signal at Dusterberry Way
  • New traffic signal at Thornton Ave./Oak St.
  • New pedestrian flashing beacon at Artist Walk driveway
  • Transit stop enhancements
  • New on-street parking spaces on Fremont Blvd.
Project Schedule

• Award Construction Contract:  Fall 2024
  • Begin Construction:  Spring 2025
  • Complete Construction:  Spring 2026

Flashing beacons are warning beacons installed at uncontrolled pedestrian crossings. Flashing beacons are a rapid flashing pattern to alert drivers when pedestrians are ready to cross.
As a driver:

Fremont Boulevard and Norris Road PHB
Pedestrian Hybrid Beacon - aka HAWK signal
Pedestrian signals provide a protected crossing opportunity on major roadways where traffic volumes do not justify a full traffic signal.
As a driver:

• You may proceed without stopping if the signal is dark.
  • Treat a solid yellow like a normal traffic signal yellow light.
  • Slow down and stop if safe to do so.
  • Treat a solid red like a normal traffic signal red light.
  • Treat a flashing red like a stop sign. Wait for any pedestrians to finish crossing, and then proceed when safe.
  • Stop at the marked stop bar (white bar across vehicle lanes).
As a pedestrian:

• Use the pedestrian push button and countdown signal like at a normal traffic signal.
  • Do not attempt to begin crossing on a flashing “Don’t Walk”.

BART Way at Civic Center Avenue
Protected intersection

Protected intersections are intersections in which bicyclists and pedestrians are separated from cars. Protected intersections shorten crossing distances, ensure cars take turns at safe speeds, and provide a more comfortable bike facility.
As a pedestrian:
• Be aware bicyclists may be present in or near crosswalks at intersections.
As a driver:

• Yield to bicyclists and pedestrians before making a right turn, as at a normal intersection.
  • Check to make sure right turns on red are not prohibited.

data.alt: BART Way and Gateway Plaza Multimodal Improvements

data.text: BART Way and Gateway Plaza Multimodal Improvements
Multimodal improvements

Phase 1 of the project was the Capitol Avenue Extension Project from Fremont Boulevard to State Street construction. Phase 2 of the project was Capitol Avenue Improvements from State Street to Paseo Padre Parkway. Phase 3 of the project improved BART Way and Gateway Plaza through the Gateway Shopping Center to provide and enhance bicycle and pedestrian connections between the Fremont BART Station and nearby employment/retail centers, housing, and Downtown.
These improvements align with the City's Capital Improvement Program, General Plan, and Downtown Community Plan goals.
The City of Fremont project consists of providing bicycle and pedestrian improvements on BART Way from the BART station to Civic Center Drive and on Gateway Plaza.
The project:

• Reconstructed the existing sidewalks with wider colored concrete sidewalks;
  • Installed decorative street and pedestrian lights;
  • Improved the Civic Center Drive intersection by providing bulb outs and a new traffic signal;
  • Rehabilitated the existing asphalt pavement by repairing base failure areas and then ground and overlayed the existing pavement with minimum 2 inches of hot mix asphalt (HMA);
  • Installed green bike lanes on BART Way
Fremont Boulevard Multimodal Corridor Program
Fremont Boulevard Multimodal Corridor

• The Fremont Boulevard Multimodal Corridor program seeks to improve bicycle and pedestrian connectivity, safety, and comfort within Fremont’s Downtown/City Center Priority Development Area (PDA), Centerville Transit PDA, and Irvington Transit PDA. This area includes the Fremont BART Station, the Centerville Train Depot (serving the ACE and Capitols/Amtrak systems), the planned Irvington BART Station, and access to AC Transit. The corridor also provides connections to American High School, Washington High School, Thornton Middle School, and Centerville Middle School.

• The corridor includes a collection of past and current complete street projects along and connecting to Fremont Boulevard. The corridor area is bounded by American High School to the north and the future Irvington BART Station to the south. The corridor’s goal is to encourage mode shift to active transportation and transit use, and to ultimately support the City’s vision of “strategic urban” development in the Downtown, Centerville, and Irvington districts of Fremont.

data.alt: Niles Boulevard and Rancho Arroyo Parkway Improvements

data.text: Niles Boulevard and Racho Arroyo Parkway Improvements
Multimodal improvements

The City of Fremont has finished a "Safe and Complete Streets" project on Niles Boulevard between Niles Bridge and Hillview Drive. The project aims to improve safety on a corridor with a history of serious traffic crashes and excessive speeding and provide quality facilities for all roadway users.
The projects feature the following:

• Traffic signal at the Rock Ave and Niles Blvd intersection
  • Flashing beacons on Niles Blvd at the pedestrian crossings at Rancho Arroyo Pkwy and El Portal Ave
  • Vehicle travel lanes narrowed to help reduce speeds on Niles Blvd.
  • Protect bike lanes from vehicle lanes with low-profile plastic curbs
  • Minimize the motorist/vehicle impacts at each intersection while still providing safety improvements at the crossing locations by maintaining four vehicles thru lanes on Niles Blvd, to provide unobstructed right turn movements, and to minimize the extent of the bulb-outs at the intersections.
Walnut Avenue Multimodal Improvements Phase 1
Multimodal improvements

Walnut Avenue serves as the primary east-west corridor in the City Center providing multimodal connections to the Downtown BART station, health care facilities such as Kaiser and Washington Hospital, Fremont government offices, School for the Deaf and School of the Blind, and numerous commercial and retail centers.
The Walnut Avenue Bikeway Improvement Project between Mission Boulevard and Paseo Padre Parkway is Phase 1 of the protected bikeway improvements on Walnut Avenue and will feature:

• Class IV (raised) asphalt concrete protected bikeways on 1.3 miles of Walnut Avenue on both sides of the street;
  • Protected intersection with signal modifications at Paseo Padre Parkway, Civic Center Drive, Guardino Drive and Gallaudet Drive
  • Pedestrian flashing beacon mid-block crossing signal on Walnut Avenue at the BART driveway
  • Incorporate bus stop landing areas along the bikeway corridor;
Watch the video, Introducing the Walnut Avenue Bikeway
Watch the video, How to use the Walnut Avenue Bikeway
Walnut Avenue Multimodal Improvements Phase 2
Multimodal improvements

The Project seeks to improve pedestrian and bicycle connectivity, safety, and comfort within the City's Downtown/City Center Priority Development Area (PDA), connecting hundreds of higher-density and affordable housing units to local shopping, social services, recreational destinations, and regional transit stops (e.g., Fremont BART Station).

The Project is part of a multi-year City effort to implement a comprehensive and connected active transportation network for all ages and abilities in the Downtown District, with enhanced bicycle and pedestrian facilities along Walnut Avenue and Fremont Boulevard serving as the main spine corridor to connect the various Downtown destinations and housing developments to the Fremont BART station.
Key Project elements include the following:

• Raised bikeways along both sides of Walnut Avenue
  • Enhanced pedestrian crossing at the Walnut Avenue/California Street intersection,
  • Bus stop/shelter upgrades along Walnut Avenue within the project limit.
Dumbarton to Quarry Lakes Trail Project

The Dumbarton Bridge to Quarry Lakes Trail will provide an east-west regional trail connection between San Mateo/Santa Clara Counties and Alameda County.  The trail will provide access to priority development areas (PDAs), transit centers, regional open spaces, and urbanized neighborhoods and form a significant link in the overall Alameda County and regional trail network.
The trail corridor is approximately 8 miles in length and will generally be comprised of paved Class I multi-use pathways, Class IV separated bikeways, protected intersections, and wide sidewalks.
Trail Animation video
East Bay Greenway (Reach 6)

The East Bay Greenway is a proposed 49-mile bicycle and pedestrian trail through Alameda County that generally follows the BART corridor, encompassing the existing Ohlone Greenway in Albany and Berkeley, and ending at the county line at the south end of Fremont.
Trail project- (Reach 6) underway
Grimmer Trail Extension
This project will transform the vacant linear right-of-way between Grimmer Boulevard and the Alameda County Flood Control Channel into a multi-use trail for walking and bicycling.
The project will extend from Fremont Boulevard to Paseo Padre Parkway and will connect directly to Central Park.
Construction: Spring 2025 - Fall 2025

Innovation Bridge

This project will connect the Warm Springs/South Fremont BART Station and thousands of jobs and housing units within Fremont’s Innovation District. This bicycle and pedestrian path is a critical link in Fremont’s multimodal transportation network.
Construction: Spring 2026 - Fall 2028

data.text: I-880 Innovation Bridge &Trail Projects

The Innovation Bridge Project will connect the Warm Springs/South Fremont BART Station and thousands of jobs and housing units within Fremont’s Innovation District. This bicycle and pedestrian path is a critical link in Fremont’s multimodal transportation network (shown as cyan blue line).
Planning and design activities are funded through a $5.5 million grant from Alameda County Transportation Commission and will be complete by Fall 2024.
Funding in the amount of $77.5 million is being pursued. Subject to funding availability, project construction is proposed to start in Spring 2026 and be completed in Spring 2028.

data.text: I-880 Pacific Commons Bridge Project

The City of Fremont’s I-880 Pacific Commons Bridge Project proposes to build a bridge over I-880 just south of the Auto Mall Parkway Interchange, thereby providing pedestrians and cyclists with a safer way to cross I-880 and avoid the busy interchange at the Auto Mall Parkway area. On the east side, it will connect to an enhanced bikeway on Grimmer Boulevard and the Warm Springs BART Station area. On the west side, the project will connect to the Pacific Commons shopping center and the Fremont Technology Business Park and ultimately link to the Bay Trail. This project will close a key gap in the pedestrian and bicycle network between the Pacific Commons commercial district and the Warm Springs BART transit-oriented development district.

Sabercat Bridge and Trail Extension Project

The trail will cross the canyon of I-680, which currently divides the Irvington District, East Bay Greenway (EBGW), and future Irvington Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) Station from the Sabercat Historical Park, Ohlone College, and Fremont Hills.

Marked by an architecturally significant bicycle and pedestrian bridge over I-680, this project will create a safe and convenient Class I multi-use bicycle and pedestrian path forging a critical link in Fremont’s city-wide cycling and pedestrian network, enhancing connectivity through and to the Irvington District.

Separated Bikeways
Citywide - Various locations (shown as thinner green lines).

The City is working to construct a network of “all ages and abilities” bicycle facilities as outlined in its Bicycle Master Plan. The City develops and implements an annual project to stripe new bikeways and enhance existing bikeways on various streets citywide, as identified in the Bike Master Plan. Typical enhancements include closing gaps in bike lanes, upgrading existing bike lanes to buffered bike lanes, adding green pavement markings to highlight areas of conflict between bikes and vehicles, and installing vertical posts to create separated bike lanes. The City also implements new and enhanced bikeways as part of street resurfacing work, per its Complete Streets policy.

Protected intersection

Protected intersections are intersections in which bicyclists and pedestrians are separated from cars. Protected intersections shorten crossing distances, ensure cars take turns at safe speeds, and provide a more comfortable bike facility.
As a pedestrian:
• Be aware bicyclists may be present in or near crosswalks at intersections.
As a bicyclist:

• Yield to pedestrians at all crosswalks. Pedestrians have the right-of-way when they must cross the bike lane.
  • Make left turns in “two stages” by going straight to the far side of the intersection, and then turning left.
As a driver:

• Yield to bicyclists and pedestrians before making a right turn, as at a normal intersection.
  • Check to make sure right turns on red are not prohibited.
